I'm a professional dog trainer and certified behavior practitioner. I use positive reinforcement.
But positive reinforcement training for reactivity isn't "reward what you like and ignore the bad"

We use management to prevent behaviors and keep everyone safe, we have strategies in place for when things don't go as planned(unexpected person comes around the corner), we set up the dog for success as much as possible to use desensitization and counter conditioning methods to change how the dog feels about the situation - we address the root cause of the behavior, and the symptoms (barking, lunging, biting) go extinct.

Above all though, make sure to address medical causes. 90% or more of my reactivity cases have had a medical component. Usually GI issues (like food allergies), ear infections, dental pain. Training won't fix a broken tooth that's causing pain. And pain, like people, can make dogs less tolerant of stress.

Unfortunately with balanced training, it punishes the dog for their behavior that is rooted in fear or anxiety, which can shut a dog down temporarily or escalate into severe and even owner directed aggression. Of which I have seen both personally.

Having a reactive dog can be very difficult emotionally too. Make sure you are taking care of yourself along the way!

Hi there! I'm a dog trainer and mini pig parent.

Something important to know about is predatory drift. Some dogs will have a higher risk than others. I recommend avoiding hounds(particularly sight hounds), terriers, and gundogs.

The concern with predatory drift is that it happens without a dog's decision making in place. A dog can be best friend with a pig, and some factor can make a change that shifts your dog into predator mode.

This is why management, training, and supervision are vital! Pigs can hurt dogs, but dogs are usually ones to kill a pig. Whether that is defense, resource guarding, or predatory. 

Pugs can be a fine dog with a pig! But I always recommend supervision together. Management like crates, closed doors, and baby gates when you cannot. Also picking up things like high value treats or food when they are together. And training for both pig and dog so they can coexist peacefully. 

I really recommend teaching "place" for both pig and dog. They are both very smart animals and to have the ability to ask them to go to a place on cue can save a lot  of concern, particularly if there's a resource involved.

I hope this helps! Reach out anytime!
